claims.claim: Protein is one of the six classes of nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, water, vitamins, minerals), and the working definition is that proteins are large molecules made of chains of amino acids; every cell in the human body contains protein.
Protein's first job is building and repairing tissue: the body uses dietary protein to repair cells and make new ones, and protein is important for growth and development.
Enzymes are proteins, and enzymes carry out almost all of the thousands of chemical reactions that take place in the body.
Some hormones are messenger proteins that transmit signals to coordinate biological processes between cells, tissues, and organs.
Proteins carry and transport substances: transport proteins bind and carry atoms and small molecules within cells and throughout the body, and hemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.
Protein provides about 4 calories per gram of energy, per MedlinePlus and the OpenStax nutrition text's table (sourced to the USDA & HHS Dietary Guidelines).

A complete protein contains all the essential amino acids, while an incomplete protein lacks one or more of them; animal foods (meat, fish, poultry, eggs, dairy) tend to be complete, and most single plant foods are incomplete on their own.
Eating a variety of legumes, grains, and nuts supplies all the essential amino acids for people eating plant-based diets, and a few plant foods such as soy and quinoa are complete on their own.
Protein-rich foods include meat, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes, nuts and seeds, and soy products such as tofu; animal products are not required to get enough protein.

The body digests dietary protein down to amino acids and rebuilds them into the proteins it needs for maintenance and growth; protein is not stockpiled, and excess protein is converted to glucose or triglycerides.
Protein is a builder first and a fuel second: when carbohydrates and fats meet the body's energy needs, dietary protein is channeled to tissue repair and restoration rather than burned as fuel.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Completeness of plant proteins: OpenStax Nutrition for Nurses states that soy is the only legume classed as complete, while Harvard's Nutrition Source adds quinoa (a seed) and chia seeds as complete plant proteins and recommends a variety of plant foods each day; MedlinePlus emphasizes that essential amino acids need not be eaten at every meal and that balance over the whole day matters.
positions: OpenStax 2.3: animal proteins are complete; soy is the only complete legume; individuals on plant-based diets can achieve complete proteins by eating various legumes, grains, and nuts.

Harvard Nutrition Source: complete proteins contain all needed amino acids; incomplete ones lack one or more of the nine essential amino acids; quinoa and chia seeds are complete plant proteins; plant-based eaters should eat a variety of protein-containing plant foods.
MedlinePlus: essential amino acids must be supplied by food but do not need to be eaten at every meal; the balance over the whole day is more important.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches that most single plant foods are incomplete on their own, that soy and quinoa are complete plant sources, and that a variety of legumes, grains, and nuts across the day covers the essential amino acids. It avoids the outdated claim that plant proteins must be combined at every single meal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Protein's role as fuel: the body can and does use protein for energy (excess protein is converted to glucose or triglycerides, and muscle can be broken down in energy shortage), yet nutrition guidance treats carbohydrate and fat as the preferred fuels.
positions: OpenStax 2.3: carbohydrates and fats must meet energy needs to channel proteins specifically for tissue repair and restoration; excess protein is converted to glucose or triglycerides depending on the body's need for energy.
Harvard Nutrition Source: protein intake in the U.S. is generally more than adequate; guidance focuses on the protein 'package' and food source rather than on protein as an energy source.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson frames protein as a builder first and a fuel second: the body prefers carbohydrate and fat for energy, and burning protein for fuel sacrifices tissue that had other jobs. The 4 kcal/g figure is stated as fact without making protein out to be the body's primary fuel.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described proteins as 'a foundational concept in Nutrition' and 'a building block for later discussions' with no factual content; all such generic boilerplate was discarded and replaced with source-verified content.

The generated draft's claim that the lesson would 'connect the term to the problem it helps people solve' was not used; the lesson teaches the working definition, jobs, energy value, completeness distinction, food sources, and builder-first framing instead.
correctionsNeeded: No prior factual draft existed (nutrition is a newly initialized subject); the lesson was written from verified sources. Amino acids, energy-and-calories, absorption, and metabolism were kept as named hand-offs to sibling topics rather than taught here.

The 4 kcal per gram figure was verified against both MedlinePlus ('One gram of protein supplies 4 calories') and OpenStax Nutrition for Nurses Table 1.1 (protein 4 calories per gram, sourced to USDA & HHS Dietary Guidelines) before publication.
